Hi everyone. This talk is about our paper, Efficient Randomized Communication Without Large Monochromatic Rectangles. It is joint work of Haoyu Wang and Pei Wu, both at Penn State.

Part I

Introduction

  1. IIntroduction
  2. IIFunction construction

I will start with an introduction: the communication models we need, the role that monochromatic rectangles play in each of them, and then our result.

A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away....

A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away, two people had a very modern problem. They lived on different planets, every bit they sent was expensive, and still they had to compute something together.

The model

Two-party communication

Leia is on Yavin 4 and holds an input x. Luke is on Tatooine and holds an input y. Together they want to compute a Boolean function f of x and y.

To do this they follow a protocol. They send bits back and forth, and each bit depends only on the sender's own input and on the bits sent so far. The whole conversation is called the transcript, Pi of x, y.

Computation on each planet is free. The only cost is the length of the transcript, in the worst case, and the goal is to make it as small as possible. We write D of f for the smallest cost of a deterministic protocol that computes f.

The standard first example is Equality. Leia and Luke hold n-bit strings, and the output is 1 exactly when the two strings are equal. It helps to draw a function as a matrix: the rows are Leia's inputs, the columns are Luke's inputs. For Equality the 1-inputs are the diagonal, and everything else is a 0-input.

Now look at what a protocol does to this matrix. Each bit splits the current set of inputs in two: by rows when Leia speaks, by columns when Luke speaks. So a transcript of three bits cuts the matrix into at most eight rectangles.

For the protocol to be correct, each rectangle must be all zeros or all ones. But a rectangle that contains two diagonal entries also contains off-diagonal entries, which are zeros. So every 1-input needs its own rectangle, and there are two to the n of them. So Equality needs at least n bits of deterministic communication.

Deterministic protocols

Deterministic protocol vs. monochromatic rectangles

Fact. A deterministic protocol of cost ccc partitions X×YX\times YX×Y into at most 2c2^c2c monochromatic rectangles.
1 bit: 2222 bits: 444ccc bits: 2c2^c2c
so one of them has density   ≥2−c\;\ge 2^{-c}≥2−c
Leia's input
x∈X\xx\in Xx∈X
Luke's input y∈Y\yy\in Yy∈Y
0-input1-input

This picture is completely general. Take any function f, and any deterministic protocol of cost c.

After the first bit, the matrix is split into two rectangles.

After the second bit, into at most four.

And after c bits, into at most two to the c rectangles, one for each transcript. The transcript determines the answer, so each of these rectangles is monochromatic: f is constant on it. And since at most two to the c rectangles cover the whole matrix, one of them has density at least two to the minus c. So a cheap deterministic protocol always leaves a large monochromatic rectangle. Please keep this picture in mind. It will come back several times.

Next, nondeterminism. There is now a third character. Yoda is all-knowing: he sees both x and y.

Yoda sends a proof to Leia and Luke, and then they talk to each other to verify it. The cost is the length of the proof plus the length of their conversation.

The requirement is the usual one for NP. On a 1-input, there is some proof that makes them accept. On a 0-input, no proof can make them accept, so Yoda cannot fool them.

Nondeterminism

Non-deterministic protocol vs. rectangle covers

Fact. If {Ri}i=1h\{R_i\}_{i=1}^{h}{Ri​}i=1h​ is a minimal rectangle cover of the 1\one{1}1-inputs of fff, then
NP(f)=Θ(log⁡h)\NP(f)=\Theta(\log h)NP(f)=Θ(logh)
a rectangle cover of the 1-inputs of f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y)

In the matrix, nondeterminism has a clean meaning. Fix one proof, together with one accepting conversation. The inputs that are consistent with it form a rectangle, and this rectangle contains only 1-inputs.

Every 1-input must be accepted with some proof. So together these rectangles cover all the 1-inputs. Unlike before, they are allowed to overlap.

Conversely, if h rectangles cover the 1-inputs, Yoda can simply name a rectangle that contains the input. This takes log h bits, and Leia and Luke each check their own side. So the nondeterministic complexity is, up to a constant factor, the logarithm of the size of the smallest cover.

Let's return to Equality, or rather to its negation: Leia and Luke want to be convinced that x and y are different. Deterministically this is as hard as before.

With Yoda it becomes easy. He sends a position i where the two strings differ; that is log n bits. Leia sends her bit at this position, and Luke compares it with his own.

In the matrix, each position gives two rectangles: Leia has a zero there and Luke has a one, or the other way around. That makes two n rectangles in all.

Here n is four: this is the same sixteen-by-sixteen matrix as before. And these eight rectangles cover every entry off the diagonal. Recall that each of the sixteen ones needed a rectangle of its own; the two hundred and forty zeros are covered by just eight. So the negation of Equality has nondeterministic complexity order log n, exponentially smaller than its deterministic complexity.

And what about Equality itself? Now Yoda has to convince them that x and y are equal, so the rectangles must cover the 1-inputs, the diagonal. But here we can repeat the rectangle argument from before: a rectangle that contains two diagonal entries also contains zeros.

So every 1-input needs its own rectangle. That is two to the n rectangles, so the proof must have n bits, and Yoda is no help at all. He can cheaply prove that two strings are different, but not that they are equal.

Now we combine the two models. This is the model behind the class P to the NP, and it is the one our lower bound is about. Leia and Luke run a deterministic protocol, but now Yoda acts as an oracle.

At any point they can send him a query. A query is a yes-or-no question about the input: a predicate Q of x and y, whose 1-inputs are covered by h rectangles.

Yoda returns the exact value of Q: a single bit, zero or one. Note the difference from before. There, Yoda could only convince them of a yes. Here they also learn when the answer is no.

A query whose 1-inputs are covered by h rectangles costs log h, exactly what it would cost to verify it nondeterministically. The total cost is the cost of all queries plus the ordinary communication. And the protocol is adaptive: each query may depend on everything that has happened so far.

NP oracle

Deterministic protocol with adaptive NP\NPNP oracle

An NP\NPNP query tests a
union of rectangles.
remaining inputs ruled out query rectangles 01the oracle's answer
Transcript regions
need not be rectangles.

Here is what such a protocol does to the matrix. At the start, every input is still possible.

The first query tests a union of rectangles. If the answer is one, the remaining inputs are inside this union. If the answer is zero, they are in its complement.

The next query, which depends on the first answer, splits each part again. Now look at the leaves. In a deterministic protocol, the inputs with a given transcript always form a rectangle. Here they do not: the complement of a union of rectangles can be an arbitrary staircase shape. So the earlier argument, that a protocol partitions the matrix into monochromatic rectangles, no longer applies.

NP oracle

Deterministic protocol with adaptive NP\NPNP oracle

Theorem [Impagliazzo, Williams, CCC 2010]
If every monochromatic rectangle of fff has density at most δ\deltaδ, then
DNP(f) ≥ Ω(log⁡(1/δ))\DNP(f)\ \ge\ \Omega\big(\log(1/\delta)\big)DNP(f) ≥ Ω(log(1/δ))
every monochromatic rectangle of fff has density ≤δ\le\delta≤δ
Read backwards
a cheap protocol with an NP\NPNP oracle leaves a large monochromatic rectangle
no large monochromatic rectangle  ⟹ \ \Longrightarrow\  ⟹  hard for PNP\PNPPNP

Still, the conclusion survives. Impagliazzo and Williams proved that if every monochromatic rectangle of f has density at most delta, then the cost of f with an NP oracle is at least order log of one over delta.

Read backwards: a cheap protocol with an NP oracle, just like a cheap deterministic protocol, leaves a large monochromatic rectangle. This is known as the product method. So to prove that a function is hard even with an NP oracle, it is enough to show that it has no large monochromatic rectangle. This is exactly what we will do.

The last model is randomized communication. We are back to Leia and Luke alone.

But now they share a public random string r, and their messages may depend on it.

On every input, they must output f of x, y with probability at least two thirds; in other words, the worst-case error is at most one third. The cost is again the length of the transcript, and we write R of f for the smallest possible cost. For example Equality, which needs n plus one bits deterministically, costs only a constant number of bits with randomness: Leia and Luke compare a few random parities of x and y.

The question

Does every cheap protocol leave a large rectangle?

Question. Does R(f)≤c\Rr(f)\le cR(f)≤c imply a monochromatic rectangle of density ≥2−O(c)\ge 2^{-O(c)}≥2−O(c) as well? [Chattopadhyay, Lovett, Vinyals, CCC 2019]

Let me summarize what we have seen. If f has a deterministic protocol of cost c, or even a protocol with an NP oracle of cost c, then f has a large monochromatic rectangle: its density is at least two to the minus order c.

The natural question is whether the same holds for randomized protocols. If f has a randomized protocol of cost c, must it have a monochromatic rectangle of density two to the minus order c? This was asked by Chattopadhyay, Lovett and Vinyals. A yes would mean that, in this respect, randomized protocols look just like deterministic ones.

Gap-Hamming for n=6n=6n=6
0-input1-inputundefined

For partial functions, the answer is known to be no. Take Gap-Hamming. The output is zero if x and y differ in at most a third of the positions, one if they differ in at least two thirds, and in between the function is undefined: there is no requirement at all.

With randomness this is easy: Leia and Luke compare x and y on a constant number of random positions. So the randomized cost is constant. But by a result of Papakonstantinou, Scheder and Song, every monochromatic rectangle is exponentially small.

The catch is the grey region. A protocol may do anything on the undefined inputs, and this promise is exactly what makes the problem easy for randomness. Complexity classes such as BPP and P to the NP are about total functions, which are defined on every input, and for total functions the question remained open. The difficulty is to fill in the grey region and still keep an efficient randomized protocol.

Our result

Our result

Theorem
There exists a total Boolean function
f:{0,1}n×{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}f:{0,1}n×{0,1}n→{0,1} with
randomized communication
R(f)≤O(log⁡n)\Rr(f)\le O(\log n)R(f)≤O(logn)
every monochromatic rectangle
density ≤2−Ω(n)\le 2^{-\Omega(n)}≤2−Ω(n)
So the answer is no, even for total functions.
In a strong form
asked: density ≥2−O(c)\ge 2^{-O(c)}≥2−O(c) for c=R(f)c=\Rr(f)c=R(f)     ours: density ≤2−2Ω(c)\le 2^{-2^{\Omega(c)}}≤2−2Ω(c)

This is our result. There is a total Boolean function on two n-bit inputs, with randomized communication complexity order log n, such that every monochromatic rectangle has density at most two to the minus order n.

So the answer to the question is no, also for total functions: an efficient randomized protocol does not guarantee a large monochromatic rectangle.

And it fails in a strong form. The question asks for density two to the minus order c. For our function, c is log n, so the largest monochromatic rectangle is doubly exponentially small in c. The function is explicit, and log n is also a lower bound on its randomized complexity.

This gives two class separations. Recall the classes. BPP is the class of total functions with randomized communication polylogarithmic in n. P to the NP is the class of total functions that have a deterministic protocol with adaptive NP queries, again of polylogarithmic cost.

Our function is called Indexed Product Equality, IPE for short. Its randomized cost is order log n. And since it has no large monochromatic rectangle, the theorem of Impagliazzo and Williams gives a lower bound of order n on its cost with an NP oracle.

So IPE is in BPP, but not in P to the NP. This is the first total function that separates the two classes, and it answers a question of Göös, Pitassi and Watson. Since NP is not contained in BPP either, the two classes are incomparable.

The second corollary is about the class P to the RP. Here the oracle answers queries that have efficient randomized protocols with one-sided error.

Two facts are known. First, P to the RP is contained in BPP: each query can be simulated by running its randomized protocol, after amplification. Second, an RP query can be simulated by an NP query, with only order log n extra cost. So P to the RP sits inside both BPP and P to the NP.

Therefore our lower bound against NP oracles transfers: IPE needs nearly linear cost with an RP oracle, so it is not in P to the RP. Hence P to the RP is strictly contained in BPP. One-sided error, even used adaptively, is weaker than two-sided error. This answers a question of Pitassi, Shirley and Watson.

Construction overview

The construction follows a framework called cheat sheets. It was introduced by Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari in query complexity, and brought to communication complexity by Anshu and coauthors. I like to think of it as locate, then verify. Each player's input has two parts: Leia holds x and u, Luke holds y and v. The second parts, u and v, each define a table, with one row for every possible address.

The first parts, x and y, point to at most one candidate address, sigma. Think of sigma as a pointer into the tables.

We look up row sigma in both tables and take the XOR of the two rows. This gives a certificate, c sigma.

Finally, a verification step checks the certificate against x, y and sigma, and the function outputs one if the check passes. The point of this design: a randomized protocol can afford to locate the address first, and then verify a single certificate. A protocol that cannot locate the address has to deal with all addresses at once.

[ABDK, STOC 2016] Scott Aaronson, Shalev Ben-David, Robin Kothari. Separations in query complexity using cheat sheets.
[ABBD+, FOCS 2016] Anurag Anshu, Aleksandrs Belovs, Shalev Ben-David, Mika Göös, Rahul Jain, Robin Kothari, Troy Lee, Miklos Santha. Separations in communication complexity using cheat sheets and information complexity.

A bit more precisely. Leia holds x and u, and Luke holds y and v. Each of the four strings has n over two bits; I will write r for n over two.

There are polynomially many addresses: an address sigma is a string of d bits, where d is order log n. For every address we build four functions. The functions p and q are built from x, y and sigma. The functions a and b are built from u, v and sigma; they encode the certificate.

The problem is called Indexed Product Equality. The output is one if there is an address sigma for which the product p times a is identically equal to the product q times b, and this product is not the zero function. So verification is an identity between two products of functions. Now I have to tell you what these functions are.

Construction overview

Construction overview: main mechanisms

I
Sparse encoding

III

The construction has three ingredients, and each one has a specific job. The first is a sparse encoding. It keeps the addresses far apart from each other, so that the right address can be located by random sampling.

The second is the function spaces of Garcia and Stichtenoth. They make the product identity checkable by evaluating the functions at a constant number of random points.

The third is a strong extractor. It generates the certificates, and it is the reason why every large rectangle contains a 1-input. I will go through them one at a time, starting with the function spaces.

Mechanism II

Garcia–Stichtenoth function spaces:  {Vb}b≥1\ \{\cV_b\}_{b\ge 1} {Vb​}b≥1​

We use a family of function spaces V b, indexed by an integer b. Every function is defined on the points one to two r, and takes values in a finite field of constant size. These spaces come from algebraic geometry. One takes a curve from the Garcia–Stichtenoth tower, which has many points over a small field; then the functions on the curve whose only pole has order at most b; and one evaluates them at two r points of the curve.

We only need two properties. The first is about products: a function in V b times a function in V c lies in V b plus c.

The second: a nonzero function in V b has at most b roots. If this looks familiar, it should. Polynomials of degree at most b have exactly these two properties. The difference is that polynomials need a field as large as the number of points. Here the field has constant size, so one evaluation is a constant number of bits.

Here is how an input becomes a function. For every string x of r bits we fix a nonzero function p x in these spaces, with one requirement.

Wherever x has a one, p x has a root.

The function may have a few more roots elsewhere, but not many: p x lies in the space V b for a b that is only slightly larger than the Hamming weight of x.

Mechanism II

Garcia–Stichtenoth function spaces

Fact 1. Any nonzero function has at most a constant fraction of roots.
Used for a random point tells two different functions apart with constant probability
Fact 2.  #{roots of px} ≥ ∣x∣\ \#\{\text{roots of }\fp_{x}\}\ \ge\ \lvert \xx\rvert #{roots of px​} ≥ ∣x∣, and at most ∣x∣+δr\lvert \xx\rvert+\delta r∣x∣+δr.
Used for the roots of px\fp_{x}px​ record where x\xxx has its ones: products of functions will compare Hamming weights

So these are the two facts we will use. Fact one: a nonzero function in our spaces has roots on at most a constant fraction of the points. So if two functions are different, a random evaluation point sees the difference with constant probability. This is what makes verification cheap.

Fact two: the number of roots of p x is at least the Hamming weight of x, and only slightly more. So the roots of p x remember where x has its ones. This is what will connect the product identity to Hamming distance.

The next ingredient is a strong extractor. An extractor takes a string u from a weak random source, together with a short, uniformly random seed, and outputs bits that are close to uniform. We use the explicit construction of Guruswami, Umans and Vadhan. The source has r bits, the seed sigma has order log r bits, and the output has ell bits, where ell can be linear in r.

The guarantee is this. Whenever u has min-entropy at least r over two, the output is within one over r of uniform in total variation distance, even together with the seed. This is what the word strong means. In our construction the seed will be the address. Note that the seed is short, so there are only polynomially many seeds.

Now the certificates. For every address sigma, Leia applies the extractor to u with seed sigma, Luke does the same with v, and the certificate c sigma is the XOR of the two outputs. So the short strings u and v generate a certificate for every address. Compare this with the tables in the cheat-sheet picture: we never write a table down. The extractor computes any row on demand.

The certificate is then read as a list of field elements. We fix a basis of one of our function spaces. The first half of the certificate gives the coefficients of a function a, and the second half gives the coefficients of a function b.

This encoding is linear: the XOR of two certificates corresponds to the sum of the functions. So Leia can evaluate a and b on her half of the certificate, Luke on his half, and the values simply add up. Neither of them needs to know the other's part.

The last ingredient is the sparse encoding. To every address sigma we assign a codeword w sigma, a string of r bits, such that any two codewords differ in a constant fraction of the positions. Since there are only polynomially many addresses, such a code is easy to construct.

For each address, Luke's string y is shifted by the codeword: z sigma is y XOR w sigma. So we get polynomially many shifted copies of y, and any two of them are far apart.

Now we can define the two functions that come from the first part of the input: p is the function of x, and q is the function of z sigma. So the check at address sigma compares x with the copy z sigma.

And here is the key fact. An address sigma star can only be accepting if x is very close to its copy, z sigma star.

The reason is a count of roots. If the two products are equal, then this common function vanishes wherever x has a one, and also wherever z has a one. But it lies in a space that allows only about as many roots as the weight of x alone, or of z alone. So the ones of x and the ones of z must almost coincide. Conversely, when x and z are close, a dimension count shows that some certificate passes the check.

Now remember that the copies are far apart. So x can be close to at most one of them. This is the picture to keep in mind: polynomially many points, far from each other, and the function can only be one if x falls into a tiny ball around one of them.

The protocol follows the construction: locate, then verify. It uses order log n bits.

Step one. Using public randomness, Leia samples order log n random positions, and sends x on these positions to Luke.

Step two. Luke knows y, so he knows all the shifted copies. He picks the address sigma star whose copy agrees best with x on the sampled positions. If there is an accepting address, its copy is much closer to x than every other copy, and order log n samples are enough to tell it apart from all the polynomially many others.

Step three. Luke sends this address back to Leia. This is another order log n bits.

Step four: verify. They sample a constant number of random points. Each of them evaluates their own part of the functions at these points. Leia sends her values, which is a constant number of field elements, and Luke checks that a is not zero there and that the two products agree. If the identity is false, the two sides differ on a constant fraction of the points, so the check fails with constant probability. In total, order log n bits.

Finally, why there is no large monochromatic rectangle. There are two things to show: every large rectangle contains a 0-input, and every large rectangle contains a 1-input.

The first one is easy. We just saw that a 1-input forces x to be very close to one of the shifted copies of y, and there are only polynomially many copies.

For a uniformly random input, the chance that x lands that close to one fixed copy is exponentially small. Taking a union bound over the two to the d addresses, the 1-inputs have density two to the minus order n.

So there is a constant alpha such that a rectangle of density at least two to the minus alpha n is simply too large to consist of 1-inputs. It must contain a 0-input.

The other direction is the heart of the proof. Take a rectangle A times B of density at least two to the minus alpha n. We want to find a 1-input inside it. Remember that Leia's input is a pair x, u, and Luke's input is a pair y, v.

Step one is a cleanup. For each x, let A x be the set of strings u such that the pair x, u is in A. We keep only those x that have many partners u, at least two to the r over two. The same for y and B y. Since the rectangle is large, most of it survives.

Step two: locate. The surviving x's and y's still form large sets, and in the Hamming cube two large sets always contain two points that are close. Applying this to the x's and to the shifted copies of the y's, we get an address sigma, and an x and a y in our sets, with x very close to z sigma. As we saw, a close pair has an accepting certificate; call it c star.

Step three: realize this certificate. We need u in A x and v in B y whose extractor outputs XOR to c star. This is where the extractor comes in. The set A x is large, so a uniform element of it has high min-entropy, and at almost every address its extractor outputs cover more than half of all certificates. The same holds for B y. Now we have two sets that each contain more than half of all certificates. Shifting one of them by c star does not change its size, so they must intersect. This gives u and v whose certificate is exactly c star, and x, u, y, v is a 1-input inside the rectangle. One detail I skipped: the address must be good for both sides at once. This is handled by averaging over the address, before the close pair is chosen.

May the force be with you.
a total function with  R(f)=O(log⁡n) \ \Rr(f)=O(\log n)\  R(f)=O(logn)  and every monochromatic rectangle of density  ≤2−Ω(n)\ \le 2^{-\Omega(n)} ≤2−Ω(n)
BPP⊈PNP\BPP\not\subseteq\PNP\quadBPP⊆PNP and PRP⊊BPP\quad\PRP\subsetneq\BPP\quadPRP⊊BPP for total functions

To conclude: we constructed a total function with logarithmic randomized communication and no large monochromatic rectangle. This separates BPP from P to the NP for total functions, and shows that P to the RP is strictly weaker than BPP. Thanks for listening, and may the Force be with you.
